sections.title: 听力 A · 1—4
sections.transcript: Lucy makes ceramic cups and planned to rent the largest stall at the town craft fair. It stood near the entrance and looked impressive in photographs. Then she calculated that the fee would consume most of the money she could reasonably earn. The organiser introduced her to Hana, who sells printed cards and also wanted a smaller commitment. They agreed to share a medium stall. Before paying, they marked the table dimensions on Lucy's floor with tape. This revealed that tall cup displays would hide Hana's cards. They changed the arrangement: cups will stand on the left at table height, while cards will hang on a light screen to the right. Lucy originally intended to bring every design she had made. Hana persuaded her to select four ranges and keep replacement stock in boxes below. They will use separate payment signs but one shared wrapping area. Lucy still worries about speaking to a crowd. She has prepared two short explanations of how the cups are made. For her, the fair is now a chance to learn which products interest buyers, rather than a test she must pass with maximum sales.

options: Its fee would take most expected earnings.
The organiser reserved it for cards.
questions.explanation: 大摊位费用会占去大部分预期收入。

questions.prompt: What did marking the table size reveal?
options: The cups might hide the cards.
The table was beside the exit.
The fair allowed one payment sign.
questions.explanation: 地面模拟显示高杯架会挡住卡片。

questions.prompt: How many product ranges will Lucy display?
questions.explanation: 她决定只展示四个系列。

questions.prompt: How does Lucy now view the fair?
options: As proof she should open a shop.
As a way to sell all her stock.
As an opportunity to learn about buyers.
questions.explanation: 结尾把展会看作了解顾客兴趣的机会。

sections.title: 听力 A · 5—8
sections.transcript:
W: Ethan, did you book the career lecture?
M: I read the outline and realised it covered information already available in the guide. I need practice answering interview questions, so I chose the smaller workshop instead.
W: What happens there?
M: We record a two-minute answer, watch it without sound, and note our body language. Then a partner listens and identifies one clear point and one confusing point.
W: That sounds uncomfortable.
M: It is, but the group has only six people. The tutor says we should improve one feature at a time rather than rewrite every answer.
W: Have you prepared?
M: I recorded myself describing a difficult team project. My first answer lasted five minutes and included unnecessary background. I shortened it, but I am keeping the specific example of how we solved a delivery problem.
W: When is the workshop?
M: Friday afternoon. I nearly chose Tuesday, but that session focuses on written applications. I will bring the job description because feedback is more useful when the group knows what the employer is seeking.

questions.prompt: Why did Ethan choose the workshop over the lecture?
options: He needed practice rather than repeated information.
The workshop had a famous speaker.
questions.explanation: 讲座内容已读过，他更需要回答练习。

questions.prompt: What do participants do before listening to a recorded answer?
questions.explanation: 先静音观看，观察肢体语言。

questions.prompt: What was wrong with Ethan's first practice answer?
options: It was too long and contained extra background.
questions.explanation: 五分钟且背景信息过多。

questions.prompt: Why will Ethan bring the job description?
options: To make feedback relevant to the employer's needs.
questions.explanation: 了解岗位需求后反馈才更有针对性。

sections.title: 听力 A · 9—12
sections.transcript: The Riverside Theatre will offer a relaxed performance of The Long Journey this Sunday at three. The story and actors are unchanged, but several features have been adjusted for audience members who find ordinary performances uncomfortable. Sudden lighting changes will be reduced, and the auditorium doors will remain open so people may leave and return. Sound effects will be quieter, although the songs will keep their original volume. The theatre's main booking page still shows only standard seating. For accessible spaces, telephone the access coordinator by Friday noon. Wheelchair users may bring one companion without an additional charge. A quiet room beside the entrance will contain chairs, water and a screen showing the performance without sound. It is not childcare, and children using it must remain with an adult. The café opens at two, but hot food will not be served before the performance because kitchen repairs continue. Drinks and cold sandwiches are available. After the show, two actors will answer questions for twenty minutes. Audience members may submit written questions at the information desk if they prefer not to speak publicly.

questions.explanation: 音效降低，但歌曲音量保持原样。

questions.prompt: How should accessible seats be booked?
questions.explanation: 无障碍座位需在周五中午前致电协调员。

options: They must stay with an adult.

questions.explanation: 明确说明儿童必须由成人陪同。

questions.prompt: What food can be bought before the performance?
questions.explanation: 厨房维修，只有饮料和冷三明治。

sections.title: 听力 A · 13—16
sections.transcript: Sam began selling unwanted household items online during a move. Listing his old desk was worthwhile: one buyer collected it the next day. Encouraged, Sam photographed every cup, book and cable separately. A week later he had spent hours answering questions about objects worth very little. Several answers were already in his descriptions. A friend suggested the Sunday community sale, where one table cost five pounds. Sam grouped books by price, tied cables into labelled bundles and took only objects that could fit in two boxes. He left the desk chair online because carrying it without a confirmed buyer made little sense. At the sale, a customer bought six books after discussing gardening with him. The cables attracted no interest, but a repair volunteer accepted them for a workshop. Sam earned less than his first optimistic estimate. However, everything was finished in one morning and the unsold cups went directly to a charity stall beside his table. He now chooses a selling method by considering time, transport and the likely value of an item, instead of assuming that a larger online audience always produces the best result.

questions.prompt: Which online sale encouraged Sam initially?
questions.explanation: 旧书桌第二天即售出，使他受到鼓舞。

questions.prompt: Why did online listing become inefficient?
options: Low-value items required too much time.
questions.explanation: 为低价值物品逐一拍照答疑耗时过多。

questions.prompt: Why did Sam leave the chair online?
options: It was difficult to transport without a buyer.
He wanted to repair it first.
questions.explanation: 没有确定买家时搬运椅子不划算。

questions.prompt: What lesson did Sam learn?
options: Every object needs an individual listing.
Selling choices should include time and transport costs.
questions.explanation: 结尾明确把时间、运输和物品价值一起考虑。

sections.title: 听力 A · 17—20
sections.transcript:
W: Lily, are you continuing the museum's recorded art-history course?
M: Yes, but I have added the monthly object session. I could remember artists' names from the videos yet had trouble discussing an unfamiliar object.
W: What did you examine last time?
M: A wooden bowl. We were not told its age at first. We described marks, repairs and signs of use, then suggested what questions we would ask a curator.
W: Did anyone guess correctly?
M: Two people identified its region, but the tutor said evidence mattered more than a lucky answer. The label was revealed only at the end.
W: Are the sessions included in the online fee?
M: No, each costs eight pounds. Places are limited to ten because everyone handles the object. Last month I waited too long and the session filled.
W: How will you avoid that?
M: The timetable is released on the first Monday of each month. I have set a reminder for nine that morning. The videos give me useful background, but examining a real object makes me notice details I would otherwise pass over.

questions.prompt: Why did Lily add the object sessions?
options: She could not remember any artists.
She wanted practice discussing unfamiliar objects.
questions.explanation: 她记得知识但不会分析陌生实物。

questions.prompt: What did learners do before seeing the bowl's label?
questions.explanation: 先观察痕迹、修补和使用证据。

questions.prompt: Why are places limited to ten?
questions.explanation: 为保证每人能接触实物而限额。

questions.prompt: When will Lily try to book?
options: At the end of each session.
At nine on the first Monday of the month.
questions.explanation: 她设定每月第一个周一九点提醒。

sections.title: 听力 B · 21—25
sections.transcript: A workplace mentoring scheme founded in 2022 is accepting new participants. Meetings happen at the community college each Thursday between 6:30 and 8:00. Membership is twelve pounds per year and free for anyone below eighteen. Applicants fill out a blue reception form and supply one photograph. In the first month, members may borrow two career books; the limit then rises to four. October's practical workshop teaches people how to give and receive useful feedback. No management experience is needed. Doors close when the session begins, so participants should arrive ten minutes before 6:30. Programme coordinator Maya Chen handles questions; college reception cannot match mentors. Before each meeting, members write one issue they want to explore. Mentors offer questions and examples rather than making decisions for somebody else. A short guide is revised each spring, using comments from both partners. The organisers remind applicants that mentoring works only when each person prepares, listens carefully and completes agreed actions between meetings. Matching normally takes three weeks. Participants may request a different mentor after the first meeting without giving a detailed reason. Conversations remain private unless someone reports an immediate safety risk.

sections.title: 阅读 A · 26—30
sections.text:
The most serious difficulty was that storage space was limited and expensive. Rather than insisting on the draft, Noah invited users to describe exactly when and why the difficulty occurred. Their answers were more useful than a simple satisfaction score. Some people valued convenience, others needed clear instructions, and several wanted enough time to become familiar with the change.

When Noah first became involved with the cooperative shop, the plan was to extend the product range immediately. The early suggestion seemed workable and attracted early support. Observation during the trial showed that unusual products attracted attention but remained unsold. The underlying aim still had value. It showed that the organisers had understood the goal more clearly than the daily experience of the people expected to take part.

The team therefore decided to study which basic items members buy repeatedly. They also agreed to test new goods in small quantities. During the following month, participation increased and fewer people asked staff for emergency help. A set of small revisions, rather than costly equipment, produced the improvement.

The evidence had clear limits. The revised system did not suit everyone, and the organisers continued to offer an alternative. They also avoided treating the first month's increase as final proof. Seasonal habits and publicity could both affect the figures.

In the organiser’s view, the lasting lesson was simple: customer interest and actual demand are different things. A project can sound excellent in a meeting and still create unnecessary barriers in practice. Careful observation gives people a chance to improve an idea without abandoning its purpose. It also makes success easier to define: not as perfect agreement, but as a service that more people can use with confidence. The experience also reminded those involved that small practical details can strongly influence whether a good idea works. Rather than making quick claims, the organisers continued to collect comments and adjust the project carefully. Members can request one trial item through a suggestion card, but repeat orders depend on sales across four weeks and available storage space.

The team therefore decided to let volunteers choose and practise roles earlier. They also agreed to send one clear role sheet in advance. During the next four weeks, more residents took part and staff received fewer requests for emergency help. A set of small revisions, rather than costly equipment, produced the improvement.

When Emma joined the work with the festival volunteer team, the plan was to assign jobs on the event morning. At the outset, the idea looked promising and won approval from several members. Observation during the trial showed that new helpers felt anxious when instructions arrived in a crowd. The underlying aim still had value. It showed that the organisers had understood the goal more clearly than the routine experience of the people expected to take part.

The central obstacle was that experienced volunteers answered conflicting questions. Rather than insisting on the draft, Emma asked participants to describe exactly when and why the difficulty occurred. Those detailed accounts proved more informative than a simple rating alone. Some people valued convenience, others needed clear instructions, and several wanted enough time to become familiar with the change.

The early evidence required caution. The revised system did not suit everyone, and the organisers kept providing an alternative. They also avoided treating the first month's increase as final proof. Seasonal habits and publicity could both affect the figures.

In the organiser’s view, the main conclusion was clear: preparation allows volunteers to be friendly as well as efficient. A project can sound excellent in a meeting and still create unnecessary barriers in practice. Close observation gives people a means of refining an idea without abandoning its purpose. It also makes success easier to define: not as perfect agreement, but as a service that more people can use with confidence. The experience also reminded those involved that small practical details can strongly influence whether a good idea works. Rather than making quick claims, the organisers continued to collect comments and adjust the project carefully. Team leaders rehearse radio messages and meeting points before opening day, leaving them more attention for visitors who need calm, accurate directions.

sections.title: 阅读 A · 36—40
sections.text:
The most serious barrier was that shared desks were crowded on the same two days. The coordinator chose not to defend the original design, Victor invited users to describe exactly when and why the barrier occurred. Their answers were more effective than a simple satisfaction score. One group prioritised convenience, another required clear instructions, and a third group asked for enough time to become familiar with the change.

Even so, the figures were not conclusive. The revised system did not suit everyone, and the initiative team kept another option available. Nor did they regard the first month's increase as final proof. Weather, calendars and publicity could influence the figures.

At the point when Victor started working on the remote-work trial, the stated objective involved require everyone to work from home three days. Initially, the proposal looked convincing and attracted early support. Evidence gathered during testing demonstrated that some employees needed equipment available only in the office. That finding did not destroy the purpose of the scheme. It showed that the initiative team had understood the goal more clearly than the daily experience of the residents expected to take part.

The revised approach was to let teams select days according to their tasks. A second decision was to coordinate attendance within each team. Over the next four weeks, participation increased and fewer residents asked staff for emergency help. Several inexpensive adjustments together created the better result.

In the organiser’s view, the lasting lesson was simple: flexibility needs coordination to remain effective. An idea may appear excellent in a meeting and still create unnecessary barriers in practice. Careful observation gives residents a chance to improve an idea without abandoning its purpose. Success then becomes easier to define: not as perfect agreement, but as a service that more residents can use with confidence. The experience also reminded those involved that small practical details can strongly influence whether a good idea works. Rather than making quick claims, the initiative team continued to collect comments and adjust the initiative carefully. Booking data is reviewed alongside task diaries, since attendance alone cannot show whether home days improved concentration or merely moved interruptions online.

sections.title: 阅读 B · 41—45
sections.text:
Five local people respond to proposed evening opening at the town arts centre.

Anna: I finish work at 5:45, exactly when the galleries close. Keeping them open on Thursday would make a public collection available to working residents. I do not expect access every night.

Ben: Visitors need technicians, receptionists and safety staff, not merely an unlocked door. The council must budget for proper evening shifts. Overloading the current team would weaken daytime services too.

Clara: A late concert series once failed because publicity stayed inside the centre. After cafés displayed posters, tickets sold quickly. Announcements must reach new audiences before organisers conclude that nobody is interested.

David: People in outer villages cannot use a 9 p.m. closing time when their last bus leaves at seven. Coordinating one event with rural transport would make the change more inclusive.

Eva: The reading gallery gives me a calm place to draw. If every evening becomes a noisy workshop, that benefit disappears. Group events and quiet individual space can coexist with thoughtful room planning.

These views favour cultural access while identifying different barriers. A successful trial must record who cannot attend as carefully as it counts those who enter. The review will therefore measure public benefit as well as ticket income. Any permanent change requires council approval after the findings are shared. A ten-week Thursday trial would keep two galleries, the studio and café open until nine. Free entry would continue, while workshops might charge for materials. Visitor figures would be recorded hourly and compared with bus arrivals, event times and weather. The centre also plans interviews with people who registered but did not attend. That evidence could reveal transport, caring duties or unclear information hidden by a simple door count. The quiet gallery would close only during one monthly performance. Rural residents could reserve seats on a return minibus if enough people register by Tuesday. After the trial, staff and community representatives would review access, cost and working conditions together.

sections.title: 阅读 C · 46—55
sections.text:
A local makers' network needs [46] planning to remain useful. Meeting rooms should be [47] for messy activities, and [48] routines protect shared equipment. Online notices [49] booking details, while volunteer advice is [50] to first-time sellers.

Initially, there was a weak [51] between skilled makers and nearby schools. Short, [52] demonstrations helped [53] uncertainty. They also [54] young people to [55] in weekend sessions.

Members contribute a small fee for materials and list any tools they can lend. Borrowers photograph equipment before use and report damage honestly. Each workshop reserves two places for people who cannot afford the full charge. The network also runs a quarterly market, but it does not judge success only by sales. Participants record new contacts, techniques learned and materials reused. Feedback led to shorter sessions for beginners and clearer ventilation rules. By combining creative freedom with dependable procedures, the group has made unfamiliar crafts less intimidating and strengthened cooperation among people who previously worked alone. A shared calendar prevents two noisy activities using the same room. Members may propose changes at monthly meetings and vote on equipment priorities. Experienced members rotate supervision so responsibility does not fall on one person. Schools may request a demonstration, but teachers remain responsible for pupils. These arrangements allow creative work to happen within clear, shared boundaries.

sections.title: 写作 · 56

chart.title: the percentage of consumers buying second-hand goods monthly

questions.prompt: Write an essay of about 120 words based on the chart. Describe and interpret the chart briefly, and give your comments.
questions.explanation: 先概括五年总体趋势并引用起止数据，再解释可能原因，最后给出个人评价和一至两项可行建议。

sections.model: The chart shows changes in the percentage of consumers buying second-hand goods monthly over five years. Overall, the figure moved steadily from 15% in 2021 to 45% in 2025. The clearest change occurred in the middle of the period, suggesting that more people gradually accepted this choice. In my view, the trend is encouraging because it reflects greater attention to convenient and responsible daily habits. However, rising numbers alone do not guarantee a good experience. Organisers should maintain reliable facilities, publish simple guidance and collect feedback from different users. They should also keep an alternative for people who cannot use the service easily. With careful management, the positive trend can continue and bring lasting value to the wider community.
